description: We’re a CS-student-led team from the University of Łódź that ships working software fast. Our lead won 1st place at a 24h hackathon with a Spring Boot web app. We want to turn NASA open data into a usable product, not just a pitch deck. Stack: Java/Spring Boot, web, data analysis. Looking for: a frontend dev (React), a data/ML person comfortable with Python, and a designer/storyteller for the demo video. Languages: EN, PL, UA, RU. Motivated beginners welcome.
summary: Crew Health Assistant is a visual, tablet-first tool that lets astronauts check their own health during a mission and tells them what to do about it. It compares every crew member with their own pre-flight baseline, not population averages, and color-codes each body system GREEN / AMBER / RED: heart, sleep, mood, bone & muscle, eyes and radiation. Every problem opens an action card explaining what is happening, why it matters in space, and 2–3 simple "do now" steps, each citing a NASA source. Because distance from Earth changes who can help, escalation advice adapts to the mission: on the ISS the crew calls the flight surgeon; in Mars transit, with a 24-minute round trip, the card tells them to start the protocol themselves and message ground in parallel. A radiation module replays a real 2017 solar particle event from NASA's DONKI database. All rules are transparent and kept in data files, with no AI at runtime. On long missions astronauts carry more of the responsibility for spotting problems early; this tool shows how that can be done clearly and safely.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

- Self-assessment at a glance: one card per astronaut and six body-system tiles (heart, sleep, mood, bone & muscle, eyes, radiation), color-coded GREEN / AMBER / RED, each with the latest value, a plain-language comparison ("Resting heart rate 74 bpm — 16% above your baseline of 64") and a sparkline.

- Personal baselines: an indicator turns AMBER when it leaves the astronaut's own band or moves the wrong way 3 days in a row, and RED when it crosses a safety limit. This catches slow drifts a single reading would miss.

- Guidance, not just numbers: each alert opens an action card with What's happening, Why it matters in space, 2–3 numbered Do-now steps (big text, big buttons), Escalation, and a linked NASA source.

- When to involve flight surgeons: escalation wording follows the mission context (ISS live link, lunar surface, Mars transit with a 12-minute one-way delay) and updates live. Routine AMBER cards say "monitor and re-measure tomorrow".

- Dynamic charts: a 30-day trend per indicator with the personal baseline band and the safety limit.

- Radiation: current and projected dose against NASA's 600 mSv career limit; a replayed NASA DONKI solar particle event turns the whole crew RED and opens the storm-shelter card.

HOW IT ADDRESSES THE CHALLENGE

Visual self-assessment; treatment and improvement guidance; indicators that can be measured in space (resting heart rate, HRV, blood pressure, sleep, mood, exercise, near-vision self-check); how spaceflight hazards affect them; when a result needs the crew or flight surgeons; different environments (station, Moon, Mars transit); dynamic charts, color coding and simple explanations.

HOW IT WORKS

Java 21 / Spring Boot REST API with a deterministic simulator and a rule engine. Thresholds, action cards and mission profiles live in JSON data files, so they can be reviewed without touching code. Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Chart.js, tablet-first with a phone layout. Packaged with Docker, deployed on Render, 13 automated tests.

NEXT STEPS

Crew self-entry and wearable feeds instead of simulated data, measurement reminders in the daily schedule, clinician-reviewed thresholds, offline operation on a crew tablet.

LIMITATIONS

Crew data is simulated. Indicator limits are illustrative, not clinical. The radiation model is simplified. Decision support only, not a diagnosis and not a medical device.

Source code, screenshots and full source list: https://github.com/Talant2801/nasa-crew-health-assistant
